think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: An 8-month-old HIV-negative infant presents with unremitting fever, pulmonary consolidation, cervical/supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, and axillary calcified nodules refractory to multi-drug broad-spectrum antibiotics (cefoperazone-sulbactam, imipenem-cilastatin). Talaromycosis is predominantly seen in advanced HIV-infected hosts or individuals with severe primary cellular immunodeficiencies; diagnosing it in an HIV-negative infant requires recognizing the profound hypogammaglobulinemia (IgG 0.49 g/L) and dysregulated lymphocyte subsets (depressed CD8+ T cells and NK cells) pointing to an underlying inborn error of immunity (X-linked hyper-IgM syndrome from a CD40LG mutation) predisposing to opportunistic fungal bloodstream infection.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint is reached following admission triage, physical examination, baseline inflammatory markers, routine negative viral/tuberculosis tests, lymphocyte flow cytometry, immunoglobulin quantification, and baseline chest CT/ultrasound, strictly prior to send-out plasma mNGS results, microbiological blood culture identification, and CD40LG genetic exome sequencing.
3. Differential Distinctions: Refractory pyogenic bacterial pneumonia and bacteremia were suspected given high inflammatory markers and consolidation, but failed escalation to imipenem-cilastatin. Tuberculosis was considered given calcified axillary nodules, lymphadenopathy, and consolidation, but PPD and T-SPOT assays were negative. In an infant with marked hypogammaglobulinemia and recurrent infections, opportunistic dimorphic fungal bloodstream infection becomes the leading diagnosis.
case_prompt:
An 8-month-old Chinese boy is admitted with a 6-day history of persistent fever and cough. Prior to referral, he received a 5-day course of empiric antibacterial therapy at an outside hospital without clinical response; laboratory evaluation there showed a white blood cell count of 24.62 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 44.1%) and C-reactive protein of 32.4 mg/L. His parents report normal psychomotor development and physical milestones, but note recurrent respiratory tract infections since birth.

On physical examination, he appears listless with poor spirit. Vital signs show body temperature 37.3°C, blood pressure 82/54 mmHg, pulse 132 beats per minute, and respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute. Palpable superficial lymph nodes are present in the cervical and retroauricular regions. Chest auscultation reveals moist rales bilaterally. The abdomen is soft, and the liver and spleen are not palpable. Neurological examination is normal.

Admission laboratory investigations demonstrate a white blood cell count of 21.5 x 10^9/L (neutrophils 40.6%), C-reactive protein of 47.98 mg/L, and procalcitonin of 0.28 ng/mL. Serum (1,3)-beta-D-glucan assay is negative. Tuberculin purified protein derivative and interferon-gamma release assays are negative. Serological tests for human immunodeficiency virus, cytomegalovirus, herpes simplex virus, and rubella virus are all negative. Flow cytometric lymphocyte subset analysis demonstrates total CD3+ T cells of 58.57%, elevated CD19+ B cells of 35.4%, CD3+CD4+ helper T cells of 50.06%, decreased CD3+CD8+ cytotoxic T cells of 6.8% (ratio 7.36), and natural killer cells of 4.23%. Serum immunoglobulin levels reveal marked hypogammaglobulinemia with IgG of 0.49 g/L (reference 2.32–14.11 g/L) and IgA of 0.07 g/L (reference 0.0–0.83 g/L), with normal IgM of 0.94 g/L.

A chest computed tomography (CT) scan shows lung inflammation, a small right pleural effusion, foliar consolidation in the left upper lobe, calcified nodules in the bilateral axillary fossae, and multiple enlarged lymph nodes in the bilateral supraclavicular fossae. Echocardiography, abdominal ultrasound, and brain MRI are unremarkable.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered given marked leukocytosis, elevated CRP, and dense lobar consolidation; however, the infant developed escalating fevers above 39°C and rising inflammatory markers despite broad-spectrum antibacterial coverage with cefoperazone-sulbactam and imipenem-cilastatin.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The patient received antibacterial (cefoperazone sulbactam, imipenem cilastatin) treatment and supportive care, including human gamma globulin. The child's condition did not improve. Temperature exceeded 39 C, with WBC 16.5*10 9/L, N% 52.0%, and CRP 62.38 mg/L.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Considered due to the presence of calcified axillary nodules, prominent supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, and pulmonary consolidation; however, purified protein derivative (PPD) and T-SPOT assays were negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: The diagnostic pivot occurred when blood mNGS identified Talaromyces marneffei within 14 hours, subsequently confirmed by microbiological blood culture growth on day 9; combined with the detection of a hemizygous CD40LG mutation underlying hyper-IgM syndrome, targeted antifungal therapy with amphotericin B and itraconazole led to complete defervescence and recovery.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Fourteen hours later TM was identified by mNGS. Microbiological blood culture confirmed TM infection on the 9th day of hospitalization, and with the quick mNGS results (Figure 2), intravenous amphotericin B (0.1-0.5 mg/kg/day, with gradual increase every 2 days) and oral itraconazole (4 mg/kg/dose bid) were administered. The patient's condition improved dramatically.

editor_comments: Distilled strictly per Stanford MedCaseReasoning methodology. Zero pathogen names in admission prompt, with complete clinical chronology, lymphocyte subsets, and imaging findings preserved.
